eligibility_reason: Registered-report replication with new data (N = 166 Japanese learners of English) of the multi-talker (HV) phonetic training experiment of Logan et al. (1991) and the single-talker (LV) experiment (Exp. 2) of Lively et al. (1993), testing pre/post learning and the claimed high-variability generalisation benefit.

effects.original_title: Training Japanese listeners to identify English /r/ and /l/. II: The role of phonetic environment and talker variability in learning new perceptual categories
effects.original_authors: Lively, S. E.; Logan, J. S.; Pisoni, D. B.
effects.original_journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
effects.replication_study: single study (HV vs LV training groups)
effects.outcome: Generalisation of /r/-/l/ identification to a novel talker (pre-test to Generalisation 1 improvement; also the trained- vs novel-talker post-test difference)
effects.timepoint: post-test (24 h to 5 days after the 15th training session)
effects.description: Training with multiple talkers (Logan et al., 1991) produced better generalisation of /r/-/l/ identification to novel talkers than training with a single talker (Lively et al., 1993, Exp. 2), so talker variability in training is important for robust generalisation.
effects.citation_sentence: For the current study, we therefore performed such a large-scale replication of the two key experiments in the original seminal studies of Logan et al. (1991) and Lively et al. (1993). We aimed to test the claim that learners generalise more after having had phonetic training on multiple talkers.
effects.evidence: Results, Model 1: "the evidence for the interaction between test session and variability condition was ambiguous (β = 0.076, SE = 0.090, z = 0.844, p =.398; BF H(0,0.32) = 0.598"; Model 2: "we similarly found ambiguous evidence for the interaction ... BF H(0,0.27) = 1.504 ... This means that results are inconclusive as to whether the amount of variability encountered during training results in differential performance". Conclusion: "Bayes Factor analyses found that in each case the evidence for a variability benefit was ambiguous. This means that null effects are not established".
effects.notes: The HV>LV claim is a cross-paper comparison: the conclusion is drawn in Lively et al. (1993) by comparing its single-talker Exp. 2 with Logan et al. (1991)'s multi-talker experiment (Logan et al. only speculated that variation is needed). Attributed here to Lively et al. (1993); a coder could attribute it to Logan et al. (1991) or code it under both. Prediction 1 (pre-to-novel-post interaction, the authors' key test) and prediction 2 (trained- vs novel-talker interaction, 'the test most closely corresponding to the claims made in Lively et al., 1993') are two measures of one claim ('Across two different measures'), so one entry; both gave ambiguous BFs. Result changed in pass 2 from failure to inconclusive: the authors' explicit wording is mixed ('found no evidence of such effect', 'different from those of the original study' vs. 'ambiguous', 'results are inconclusive', 'null effects are not established'), and the codebook tiebreaker for doubt between failure and inconclusive is inconclusive. Failure remains a plausible reading (99% power for the original effect size; 'if it does exist, such a benefit ... is likely very small'). Replication type: authors call it a 'direct-as-possible replication'; deliberate changes (new stimulus recordings, Japan-resident online Prolific sample, counterbalanced talkers, pre-test vs generalisation-task comparison, feedback on all trials, pre-test ceiling cut-off) could support close extension. Training-phase LV-advantage hypothesis (prediction 3) is not from the originals and gets no entry.

The codebook tiebreaker (doubt between failure and inconclusive -> inconclusive) therefore applies. This was decided from the source, not from the candidates agreeing. No entries added or removed.
